script.opening: "I started a new tablet about ten days ago — lamotrigine, for my epilepsy — and now I’ve got this rash spreading everywhere, some bits blistering and the skin coming away. My mouth is full of painful sores, my eyes are red and sore, and it hurts to wee. I feel awful and feverish. Is this the tablet?"

facts.text: Started 2 days ago on her chest and face as dusky red-purple blotches, now spreading to arms and back. Some have blistered; skin on her chest peels away if rubbed — will show the camera if asked. Burning and painful rather than itchy.
Lips crusted and bleeding; mouth full of sores; swallowing hurts but can sip water. Both eyes red, gritty, sore in the light. Painful to pass urine; sores "down below".
Fever 38.6 on her thermometer, shivery, achy, weak. Breathing OK. Not confused. Passing small amounts of urine.

Lamotrigine started 10 days ago by the neurologist (had been on levetiracetam, which made her moody). Nothing else new — no antibiotics, no painkillers apart from paracetamol yesterday. On the progestogen-only pill. No known allergies before this.
Generalised seizures since age 19; last seizure 6 months ago. Not driving because of that. Worried about fitting without her tablet.
Lives with her husband, Saif, who is at work 20 minutes away; her mother lives nearby. Two children at school. Works as a pharmacy technician.

Frightened, in pain, speaking carefully because of mouth sores. You underestimate how serious it is and ask "Can’t I just have some cream?" when hospital is mentioned. Then worry about your epilepsy: "But it’s for my epilepsy — what if I have a fit?" Accept an ambulance once the danger is explained.

ice.ideas: "I think it’s an allergy to the new tablet."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — fear of having a seizure if she stops the tablet, and who will collect the children from school.
ice.expectations: "Some cream or antihistamines." Does not expect to be told it is an emergency.

cues: "Is this the tablet?" — the culprit drug, started 10 days ago.
"The skin is coming away" and "my mouth and eyes are raw" — the emergency features.
"What if I have a fit?" — her worry about stopping lamotrigine, to address while still stopping it.

checkpoints.text: Recognises SJS/TEN from the red flags — recent culprit drug, painful rash, dusky/target lesions, blistering/skin detachment (Nikolsky), and MUCOSAL involvement (mouth/eyes/genitals) with systemic illness

Identifies the likely CULPRIT DRUG (antiepileptics, allopurinol, sulfonamides/antibiotics, oxicam NSAIDs, nevirapine) and STOPS it immediately — knowing that for an antiepileptic the hospital arranges seizure cover
Recognises a life-threatening EMERGENCY and arranges IMMEDIATE admission (dermatology/burns/ITU + early ophthalmology) with a sepsis risk assessment (NICE NG253) — not community management
Knows the extent bands (SJS <10%, overlap 10–30%, TEN >30%), the differential (erythema multiforme, staph scalded skin, DRESS) and the seriousness (skin failure, fluid loss, infection, mortality)
Documents the suspected drug as a SEVERE reaction to prevent fatal re-exposure, flags related drugs for specialist discussion, and reports on a Yellow Card (MHRA)
Communicates urgency clearly but calmly to a frightened patient and arranges emergency transfer
Checks understanding of the need for hospital specialist care, avoiding both panic and false reassurance
Arranges disposition: emergency admission today (999/acute), drug stopped + allergy documented + Yellow Card, early ophthalmology/skin care flagged, clear handover

worked.txt: "I’m glad you contacted us — yes, this is very likely a serious reaction to the new tablet. The spreading blistering rash, skin coming away, and raw mouth, eyes and genitals make me think of Stevens-Johnson syndrome. That’s an emergency, not a minor rash."

"Stop the lamotrigine now and take no more. I’ll record it as a serious allergy so you’re never given it again — re-taking it could be dangerous — and I’ll report it to the medicines safety scheme. I know it’s for your epilepsy — the hospital will give you safe seizure cover straight away, today."

"You need hospital straight away — I can’t check your pulse, blood pressure or temperature over video — skin specialists, often burns-level care, and eye specialists early on, because your skin and the surfaces of your eyes and mouth need protecting. I’m arranging that now."
"When skin is affected this badly it can’t do its job — fluid loss and infection become a real risk — so this can’t wait or be managed at home."
"Don’t put creams on it, sip fluids if you can, and bring the tablet packet so they know exactly what caused it."
"If your breathing becomes difficult, you can’t swallow, or you feel very faint, call 999. The plan is hospital, now — I’ll make sure they’re expecting you."

f.learning: STEVENS-JOHNSON SYNDROME / TOXIC EPIDERMAL NECROLYSIS (SJS/TEN) is a life-threatening severe cutaneous adverse drug reaction: a recent culprit DRUG plus a PAINFUL (not merely itchy) rash with dusky/target macules, BLISTERS and skin detachment (Nikolsky+), and crucially MUCOSAL erosions of ≥2 of mouth/eyes/genitals, with fever and systemic illness (SJS <10% body-surface detachment, SJS/TEN overlap 10–30%, TEN >30% — BAD UK guidelines 2016). The combination of mucosal involvement, skin detachment and a culprit drug is the alarm. Identify the culprit (antiepileptics — lamotrigine/carbamazepine/phenytoin; allopurinol; sulfonamide/other antibiotics; oxicam NSAIDs; nevirapine), typically started days-weeks before, and STOP it immediately (for an antiepileptic the hospital arranges safe seizure cover), documenting a severe drug allergy and reporting on a Yellow Card (MHRA), since re-exposure can be fatal and prompt withdrawal improves outcome. Recognise an EMERGENCY with significant mortality (skin failure causes fluid/electrolyte loss, thermoregulation failure, infection/sepsis, eye/mucosal complications) and arrange IMMEDIATE admission — dermatology with burns/ITU-level supportive care and EARLY ophthalmology, with a sepsis risk assessment (NICE NG253; observations cannot be taken on video) — not community management. Know the differential: erythema multiforme (milder, target lesions, often post-HSV, less mucosal/systemic), staphylococcal scalded skin (mostly young children, no mucosa), and DRESS (rash, fever, eosinophilia, organ involvement). Communicate the urgency clearly but calmly, arrange emergency transfer, and ensure the drug is stopped and documented. The skill is rapid pattern recognition, stopping the drug, and emergency admission — not a community antihistamine.

knowledge.guideline: [1] UK guidelines for the management of Stevens–Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis in adults (British Association of Dermatologists, 2016) · [2] NICE NG253 (suspected sepsis in people aged 16 and over) · [3] MHRA Yellow Card scheme · [4] BNF monographs of the suspected drug (for example lamotrigine, carbamazepine, allopurinol, co-trimoxazole)
knowledge.summary: A painful spreading rash with dusky target-like patches, blisters and peeling skin, erosions of the mouth, eyes and genitals, and fever, about ten days after a new drug (here lamotrigine, started for epilepsy), is Stevens–Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis until proven otherwise. Stop the drug, send her to hospital by 999 ambulance with a call ahead, document a severe allergy, and report it on a Yellow Card.

points.t: Prodromal fever and malaise, then painful dusky red or purple macules and atypical targets that blister and detach, with erosions at two or more mucosal sites (mouth, eyes, genitals). Skin tenderness out of proportion to the rash is an early clue. Onset is typically 4–28 days after starting a new drug [1].
Body surface area of detachment: SJS below 10%, SJS/TEN overlap 10–30%, TEN above 30% [1]. Severity and prognosis are assessed in hospital (SCORTEN).

High-risk drugs include allopurinol, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, sulfonamide antibiotics such as co-trimoxazole, nevirapine and oxicam NSAIDs [1][4]. Identify every drug started in the past two months, including over-the-counter and herbal products.

Stop the suspected drug immediately; early withdrawal improves survival [1]. Arrange emergency admission — dermatology-led care, often in a burns or intensive care unit, with early ophthalmology review because eye damage can be permanent [1]. Assess for sepsis risk (NICE NG253 [2]); on video, observations cannot be taken, which lowers the threshold further.

Erythema multiforme (typical raised targets on the limbs, often after herpes simplex, limited mucosal involvement, little systemic illness); staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (mostly young children, superficial peeling, no mucosal erosions); DRESS (widespread rash, facial swelling, fever, eosinophilia and organ involvement, usually 2–8 weeks after the drug); generalised bullous fixed drug eruption.

points.h: If the drug treats something important
points.t: If the culprit is an antiepileptic, stopping it still comes first; the hospital team will arrange safe seizure cover. Never re-start it without specialist advice.

Record the drug as a severe reaction (not a simple intolerance) with the date and reaction; add a clear alert. Report on a Yellow Card [3]. The patient should carry the information and avoid the drug for life; related drugs are discussed with the specialist.

dg.d: Open question; let her describe the rash, mucosal symptoms and the new tablet before questioning.
Asked who was with her, how she would get to hospital, and about her fear; acknowledged the reason the drug was started.
Used video to inspect mouth, eyes and skin and check detachment; stated that observations and full examination need hospital.
SJS/TEN versus erythema multiforme, SSSS and DRESS; asked about HSV and previous reactions.
Checked breathing, swallowing and fluid intake; assessed sepsis risk; recognised mucosa plus detachment plus culprit drug as an emergency.
Suspected SJS/TEN from a recently started drug, explained in plain words.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Stop the drug now; 999 ambulance and call ahead to the hospital team; do not drive; bring the packet.
Explained that her epilepsy will be covered in hospital (safe seizure cover); severe allergy recorded with alert; Yellow Card report.
Escalation advice while waiting; someone to stay with her; follow-up call; teach-back.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up ‘skin coming away’, mucosal pain and ‘is this the tablet?’; responded to her fear and wish for cream.
Idea: a reaction to the tablet. Concern: the spreading blistering rash and feeling very unwell. Expectation: treatment, hoping for cream.
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — fear of having a seizure if she stops the tablet, and who will collect the children from school — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mrs Karim, I’m Dr Mensah. Can you hear and see me clearly? Tell me what’s been happening.
model.why: Checks the video link and opens

model.text: I started a new tablet about ten days ago, and now I’ve got this rash spreading everywhere, some bits blistering and the skin coming away. My mouth is full of painful sores, my eyes are red and sore, and it hurts to wee. I feel awful and feverish. Is this the tablet?

Thank you. I’m worried this could be a serious reaction to the tablet, so I’m going to ask a few quick questions and look at what I can on the camera. Then I’ll tell you exactly what we need to do. Is that okay?
model.why: Signals urgency calmly and sets a short agenda

model.text: Yes. I’m scared.
First — are you having any trouble breathing or swallowing? Are you managing to drink?
model.why: Checks airway, breathing and fluid intake first

model.text: Swallowing hurts. I can sip water. My breathing’s okay.
Can you show me your mouth, and your eyes, on the camera? … And the rash on your chest or arms? Is it painful, or itchy?
model.why: Uses video to inspect mucosa and skin; pain versus itch

model.text: (Shows crusted lips, red eyes and dusky patches with blisters on the chest.) It’s painful, it burns. Not really itchy.
If you press gently next to a blister, does the skin slide or peel off?
Yes, it comes away, look.
Can you hold the tablet box up to the camera? … Thank you. When did you start it, and what was it for? Any other new medicines or remedies in the last two months?
model.why: Identifies the culprit and all recent drugs

model.text: It’s lamotrigine, for my epilepsy — I started it about ten days ago. Nothing else new that I can think of.
Have you had anything like this before, or cold sores recently?
model.why: Screens for previous reaction and HSV-triggered erythema multiforme

model.text: Not that I can think of.

I’m going to be straight with you, because it matters. The painful rash, blisters, skin peeling and sores in your mouth, eyes and down below, after a new tablet, look like a rare but serious reaction called Stevens–Johnson syndrome. It needs hospital care today.
model.why: Names SJS/TEN and the need for admission clearly

model.text: Hospital? Can’t I just have some cream?

I understand that’s a lot to hear. Cream and antihistamines won’t be enough. The skin is a protective barrier, and when it peels you can lose fluid and pick up infection quickly, and your eyes need a specialist to protect them. Hospital teams treat this every day.
model.why: Acknowledges fear; explains why community care is unsafe

model.text: Okay. What do I do?
Three things. First, don’t take any more of the lamotrigine — not even tonight’s dose. Put the box in your bag to take with you.
But it’s for my epilepsy. What if I have a fit?

I know, and the hospital will look after your epilepsy today — they will give you safe seizure cover and an alternative if needed. Right now the reaction is the bigger danger. Second, I’m calling an ambulance for you now, rather than you getting there yourself. Please don’t drive.
An ambulance? Is it that bad?
It’s serious enough that I want you there quickly and safely. I’ll phone the hospital team so they know you’re coming. Is anyone with you, or someone you can call to be with you until it arrives?
I’ll ring someone now.

Good. Third, I’m recording lamotrigine on your notes as a serious reaction, so it’s never prescribed again, and I’ll report it to the medicines regulator on a Yellow Card. You should never take it again.
model.why: Documents a severe allergy and reports via Yellow Card

model.text: Okay.

While you wait, sip fluids if you can, and don’t burst the blisters or put creams on. If your breathing gets harder, you can’t swallow, you feel faint, confused or much worse before the ambulance comes, call 999 again straight away. Can you tell me the plan back?
No more tablets, take the box, the ambulance is coming, someone will be with me, and 999 again if I get worse.
Exactly right. You’ve done the right thing calling today. I’ll stay on the line while I arrange the ambulance, and I’ll check with the hospital tomorrow to see how you are.
model.why: Stays with her and closes the loop

model.text: Thank you. I’m glad I called.

social.t: She should not drive. Arrange a 999 ambulance, and someone to stay with her if possible.
Survivors can have eye, mouth and genital scarring and psychological after-effects; follow-up with ophthalmology and support after discharge help.

legal.t: Report suspected serious adverse drug reactions to the MHRA through the Yellow Card scheme.

professional.t: Code it as a severe drug reaction with a prominent alert, name the drug and reaction, and tell the prescriber and community pharmacy (GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices).
Record what was seen on video and that observations could not be taken; the limits of video lower the threshold for emergency transfer.

community.t: SJS Awareness UK for patient information and peer support after discharge.

redFlags: Mucosal erosions at two or more sites with skin detachment after a new drug — emergency admission
Difficulty breathing or swallowing, unable to drink
Signs of sepsis (NICE NG253) — confusion, fast breathing, feeling faint
psychosocial: Worry about stopping a drug started for a reason
ice: Idea: a reaction to the new tablet
Concern: the spreading blistering rash and raw mouth and eyes
Expectation: treatment, hoping it can be managed at home

playbook.diagnosis: Suspected Stevens–Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis about ten days after starting a new drug: painful dusky rash with blistering and detachment, oral, ocular and genital erosions, fever and malaise.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “This looks like a rare, serious reaction to the tablet where the skin and the lining of the mouth and eyes become inflamed and peel. It needs hospital care today — and the most important step is stopping the tablet.”

management.reflectIce: “You wondered if it was the tablet — I think you’re right, and that’s why we stop it now.”
management.psychosocial: Calm, honest explanation; reassure that the hospital will manage whatever the drug was treating; someone to be with her.
sharedPlan: 999 ambulance to hospital with a call ahead to the on-call team; do not drive
Severe drug reaction recorded with alert; Yellow Card report
safetyNet: 999 again if breathing, swallowing, fainting or confusion worsen before the ambulance
Follow-up call to the hospital or patient the next day

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by treating a medical emergency as a skin complaint. The marks are for recognising the pattern quickly, stopping the drug and getting her to hospital safely.

items.fail: Treating it as an ordinary drug rash with antihistamine or cream.
items.why: Mucosal erosions and skin detachment after a new drug are SJS/TEN.
items.fix: Recognise the triad of culprit drug, mucosa and detachment.

items.fail: Not stopping the drug straight away.
items.fix: Stop it now; the hospital covers the underlying condition.

items.fail: Telling her to make her own way to A&E or to book a review.
items.why: She is systemically unwell and deteriorating.

items.fail: Forgetting to record the allergy or report it.
items.why: Re-exposure can be fatal; reporting is expected.
items.fix: Severe allergy alert and Yellow Card.

items.fail: Frightening her, or giving false reassurance.
items.why: Both undermine a calm, fast transfer.
items.fix: Be honest and calm, and explain why each step matters.

items.fail: Claiming a full examination over video.
items.why: Observations and a full skin check cannot be done remotely.
items.fix: Say what you saw and that hospital will do the rest.

Breathing, swallowing, fluids; mouth, eyes and skin on camera; detachment; the drug and timing; HSV and previous reactions.
Name suspected SJS/TEN; explain why hospital, not cream.
Stop the drug; 999 ambulance and call ahead; do not drive; someone with her; severe allergy recorded; Yellow Card.

wordPics.fail: Calls it a drug rash and prescribes antihistamine or steroid cream; continues the drug; books a routine review or tells her to make her own way to A&E; forgets to record the allergy.
wordPics.pass: Recognises SJS/TEN; stops the drug; arranges emergency admission; documents a severe allergy.
wordPics.exc: All of that, plus: checks airway and fluids first; uses the video well and is honest about its limits; explains calmly why hospital is needed; handles the ‘but it was started for a reason’ worry; ambulance with a call ahead; Yellow Card; someone with her; teach-back; follow-up call.

avoid.dont: “It’s probably an allergic rash — try an antihistamine and see how it goes.”
avoid.instead: “This looks like a serious reaction that needs hospital today.”
avoid.why: Mucosal erosions with skin detachment after a new drug are an emergency.

avoid.dont: “Keep taking the tablet until you see the hospital.”
avoid.instead: “Don’t take any more of it — the hospital will cover what it was treating.”
avoid.why: Early withdrawal of the culprit improves survival (BAD 2016).

avoid.dont: “Pop along to A&E when you can.”
avoid.instead: “I’m calling an ambulance now, and I’ll phone ahead.”
avoid.why: She is systemically unwell with skin failure; the route must be safe and fast.

points.t: If the culprit is an antiepileptic, stopping it still comes first; the hospital team will arrange safe seizure cover. Never re-start it without specialist advice.

Record the drug as a severe reaction (not a simple intolerance) with the date and reaction; add a clear alert. Report on a Yellow Card [3]. The patient should carry the information and avoid the drug for life; related drugs are discussed with the specialist.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let her describe the rash, mucosal symptoms and the new tablet before questioning.
Asked who was with her, how she would get to hospital, and about her fear; acknowledged the reason the drug was started.
Picked up ‘skin coming away’, mucosal pain and ‘is this the tablet?’; responded to her fear and wish for cream.
Idea: a reaction to the tablet. Concern: the spreading blistering rash and feeling very unwell. Expectation: treatment, hoping for cream.
Used video to inspect mouth, eyes and skin and check detachment; stated that observations and full examination need hospital.
SJS/TEN versus erythema multiforme, SSSS and DRESS; asked about HSV and previous reactions.
Checked breathing, swallowing and fluid intake; assessed sepsis risk; recognised mucosa plus detachment plus culprit drug as an emergency.
Suspected SJS/TEN from a recently started drug, explained in plain words.
Stop the drug now; 999 ambulance and call ahead to the hospital team; do not drive; bring the packet.
Explained that her epilepsy will be covered in hospital (safe seizure cover); severe allergy recorded with alert; Yellow Card report.
Escalation advice while waiting; someone to stay with her; follow-up call; teach-back.

social.t: She should not drive. Arrange a 999 ambulance, and someone to stay with her if possible.
Survivors can have eye, mouth and genital scarring and psychological after-effects; follow-up with ophthalmology and support after discharge help.

legal.t: Report suspected serious adverse drug reactions to the MHRA through the Yellow Card scheme.

professional.t: Code it as a severe drug reaction with a prominent alert, name the drug and reaction, and tell the prescriber and community pharmacy (GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices).
Record what was seen on video and that observations could not be taken; the limits of video lower the threshold for emergency transfer.

community.t: SJS Awareness UK for patient information and peer support after discharge.

redFlags: Mucosal erosions at two or more sites with skin detachment after a new drug — emergency admission
Difficulty breathing or swallowing, unable to drink
Signs of sepsis (NICE NG253) — confusion, fast breathing, feeling faint
psychosocial: Worry about stopping a drug started for a reason
ice: Idea: a reaction to the new tablet
Concern: the spreading blistering rash and raw mouth and eyes
Expectation: treatment, hoping it can be managed at home

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Suspected Stevens–Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis about ten days after starting a new drug: painful dusky rash with blistering and detachment, oral, ocular and genital erosions, fever and malaise.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “This looks like a rare, serious reaction to the tablet where the skin and the lining of the mouth and eyes become inflamed and peel. It needs hospital care today — and the most important step is stopping the tablet.”

management.reflectIce: “You wondered if it was the tablet — I think you’re right, and that’s why we stop it now.”
management.psychosocial: Calm, honest explanation; reassure that the hospital will manage whatever the drug was treating; someone to be with her.
sharedPlan: 999 ambulance to hospital with a call ahead to the on-call team; do not drive
Severe drug reaction recorded with alert; Yellow Card report
safetyNet: 999 again if breathing, swallowing, fainting or confusion worsen before the ambulance
Follow-up call to the hospital or patient the next day

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by treating a medical emergency as a skin complaint. The marks are for recognising the pattern quickly, stopping the drug and getting her to hospital safely.

items.fail: Treating it as an ordinary drug rash with antihistamine or cream.
items.why: Mucosal erosions and skin detachment after a new drug are SJS/TEN.
items.fix: Recognise the triad of culprit drug, mucosa and detachment.

items.fail: Not stopping the drug straight away.
items.fix: Stop it now; the hospital covers the underlying condition.

items.fail: Telling her to make her own way to A&E or to book a review.
items.why: She is systemically unwell and deteriorating.

items.fail: Forgetting to record the allergy or report it.
items.why: Re-exposure can be fatal; reporting is expected.
items.fix: Severe allergy alert and Yellow Card.

items.fail: Frightening her, or giving false reassurance.
items.why: Both undermine a calm, fast transfer.
items.fix: Be honest and calm, and explain why each step matters.

items.fail: Claiming a full examination over video.
items.why: Observations and a full skin check cannot be done remotely.
items.fix: Say what you saw and that hospital will do the rest.
